title: Vegetable seller and maths wizard
author: Vijayalakshmi  Kadambari
content_html:
She is very busy especially between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m. every day when scores of us stand around her very modest selling place demanding vegetables, negotiating prices, and complaining about how long it takes for her to cater to each one of us…

Patiently, she handles all of us, putting in loads and loads of personal attention, “Oh! You are buying more today, amma! Has your daughter come for a visit from her in-law’s place?” “Saar, it s been sometime since you came this side, have you been visiting America?”,

But when it comes to negotiating prices, she is very clear. Discounts are usually reserved for regular customers only. Otherwise, it’s a strict “no”. Her maths skills beat me! Awesome! People just list out 1 kg of onions, half kg of tomatoes, green chillies, and she deftly calculates the prices at super speed. “Oh! That will be ₹250,” she declares, and immediately goes on to another customer, calculating again. Someone hands her a ₹500 note for a ₹135 bill and she hands back the exact change, the soiled notes telling the story of her toil.

The speed of her calculations put to shame many of us who quickly pull out the calculator on our smartphones to add those numbers.

Her PR skills are superb! No selling costs! Yet the intense competition she faces from her neighbour seller solely and solidly rests on brand value of the tender veggies her short-time stall sells. She does have loyal customers who wait even if it’s painstakingly long to buy from her.

The man on the other side of the stall — sometimes her husband or her son — just carries the vegetables from the small truck. Any unruly or arrogant customer gets a taste of her rustic stinging sarcasm and is immediately silenced.

Perhaps around 9.30 a.m. or so, she silently sips tea from the tiniest cup you can see and prepares to leave for the day.

Her skills are all part of on-the-job training. Her guru is a very strict teacher and she never passes out of her ‘Gurukul’, throughout her life — she belongs to the school of poverty.

title: The great Indian lie
author: Jeter  Dagam
content_html:
There are many lies in this world. Some are big. Some are dangerous. Some have changed the course of history. But none have survived as successfully as the Indian classic: “I’m reaching in 5 minutes.”

The beauty of this sentence is that everyone knows it is untrue. The person saying it knows. The person hearing it knows. Even Google Maps probably knows. Yet the tradition continues.

A friend calls and asks where you are. You confidently reply, “Just five minutes away.” In reality, you may still be in the shower, searching for your missing keys, or trying to locate the left sock that vanished under mysterious circumstances. But spiritually, mentally, and emotionally, you are indeed five minutes away.

I remember once telling a friend I was “just five minutes away” while standing in front of my cupboard trying to decide what to wear. I hadn’t left the house. I hadn’t found my wallet. Yet somehow, in my mind, I was already halfway there.

Some people say India has a rich cultural heritage. They are right. This phrase is part of it. In fact, “five minutes” is not really a unit of time. It is a state of mind. A person can remain five minutes away for forty-seven minutes without experiencing the slightest contradiction. Scientists have yet to explain this phenomenon.

What makes the phrase fascinating is that most people who use it are not deliberately trying to deceive anyone. At that moment, they genuinely believe it. They are describing not where they are, but where they intended to be. They are imagining the version of themselves who woke up on time, left the house promptly, and resisted the temptation to spend 20 minutes scrolling through videos before getting ready.

In that sense, the lie is not really told to other people. It is told to ourselves.

Human beings are remarkably skilled at living slightly ahead of reality. We rarely describe our actual situation; instead, we describe our plans. “I’ll start studying tomorrow.” “I’ll begin exercising next week.” “I’ll call them later.” Our lives are crowded with imaginary future versions of ourselves who are organised, disciplined, punctual, and productive. Unfortunately, those versions rarely arrive. The real us eventually shows up instead — late, apologetic, and carrying a phone.

Perhaps that is why the phrase has survived for generations. It is not really about time. It is about hope. Every “five minutes” contains a small act of optimism, a belief that we are closer to becoming the person we want to be than we actually are.

Reality, of course, eventually catches up. The friend waiting outside has already ordered food. The movie has started. The meeting has begun. And you are still explaining traffic conditions that somehow affected a journey you had not yet started.

Yet maybe the reason this lie survives is not because people keep telling it, but because people keep forgiving it. We rarely feel genuinely betrayed when someone says, “I’m reaching in five minutes.” We roll our eyes, complain briefly, and then wait. Deep down, we understand. We have all said it ourselves.

Perhaps that is because the phrase is not really a lie at all. It is a request for patience — a small plea for understanding between who we are and who we hoped to be.

After all, all of us are five minutes away from something: five minutes away from starting that project, making that phone call, fixing that habit, or becoming the person we keep promising ourselves we will become. The difference is that some journeys take a little longer than expected.

About 47 minutes, give or take.

title: Enjoying theatre
author: Rajani  Balaji
content_html:
The lights dimmed slowly. Conversations softened into whispers and then disappeared altogether. Hundreds of strangers sat in silence as Shurpanakhi, written by Apurva Kasaravalli and directed byVandana Supriya Kasaravalli, began to unfold at Ranga Shankara in Bengaluru. As I settled into my seat, a thought crossed my mind. In a world where everything competes for our attention, what happens when something asks for it completely?

It is a curious dilemma of our times. We complain about distraction and our inability to focus. Yet we willingly participate in systems designed to fragment our attention. There is always a notification to check, a message to respond to, a reel to watch, or a headline to scan. We are connected as never before, yet rarely fully present.

Theatre, however, demands something different. For 90 minutes, there are no shortcuts. No fast-forward button. No option to pause and return later. The performance moves at its own pace, indifferent to our impatience. If our minds wander, we miss something. Theatre does not wait for us.

Most experiences today are designed around our convenience. We can skip, scroll, replay, accelerate and customise them to suit our preferences. Theatre offers no such accommodation. It unfolds on its own terms. There is something almost radical about an art form that refuses to adapt itself to our distractions. This is perhaps the first lesson it teaches: presence.

Unlike cinema, where the camera directs our gaze, theatre leaves that responsibility to the audience. Meaning is not neatly packaged and delivered. It often resides in a pause, a silence, a fleeting expression, a subtle shift in lighting, or the distance between two characters on a stage. You learn to listen beyond words and to notice what is not immediately obvious. At first, this can feel demanding. Yet it is also rewarding.

In a culture that values speed, theatre reminds us that some things reveal themselves only when we slow down. Not every scene is dramatic. Not every exchange is loud. Some moments unfold quietly. Yet these are often the moments that stay with us long after the curtain falls. There is another quality that makes theatre distinct. What unfolds on stage is live, fragile, and unrepeatable. When an actor pauses for a fraction too long, the audience senses it. When emotion trembles in a voice, it is shared by everyone in the room. A slight mistake, a spontaneous reaction, an unexpected burst of laughter — these become part of that evening’s performance and belong only to those who were present.

Perhaps this is what makes theatre feel so intensely human. The audience, too, becomes part of the experience. A ringing phone, a whispered conversation, a glowing screen — each has the power to disrupt the shared concentration of hundreds of people. Without announcing it, theatre reminds us that public spaces depend on mutual consideration. We are not merely individuals occupying adjacent seats; we are participants in a collective experience.

At the end of the performance, the applause lingered. The actors took their bow. Many in the audience remained seated for a few moments, acknowledging the effort that had unfolded before them. Nobody seemed particularly eager to rush away. It felt like a small but meaningful act of respect in a culture that is constantly moving on to the next thing.

As I left the auditorium that evening, the dilemma remained. We spend much of our lives searching for experiences that hold our attention. Yet when something finally asks for our complete attention,we often find it difficult to give. Is the challenge that theatre demands too much of us? Or that the rest of the world demands too little?

title: Memory in the pocket
author: Sharada A.L.
content_html:
A friend recently forgot her phone at home. She wanted to call her family but could not because she did not remember a single phone number. For a while, she felt completely stranded. She had forgotten how to reach them, having quietly delegated that memory to the phone she had left behind.

That incident stayed with me because my own memory behaves very differently.

I remember phone numbers with surprising ease. Not because I have an exceptional memory, but because I look for patterns. Many numbers begin with familiar combinations. The remaining digits often have a rhythm of their own. Once I discover that rhythm, the number stays with me.

A language of its own

It made me realise that memory has a language of its own. It loves rhythm, pattern, and association. We remember songs because of their melody, poems because of their rhythm, stories because one event leads naturally to another. Even a phone number becomes memorable when it stops being a random string of digits and begins to make sense.

Names, however, are another matter.

More than once, I have been talking to a close friend and have suddenly forgotten her husband or children’s names. Once, I asked, “How are the kids?” She replied that they were doing well. Normally, I would have asked about each child individually. Instead, the conversation stopped there because I could not remember their names.

Finally, I admitted it. We laughed. But I came away with an uncomfortable thought.

It wasn’t just embarrassing. It restricted the conversation. I realised that forgetting names does not merely mean losing information. It means losing the ability to make conversations personal and meaningful.

When I address people by their names, they know I remember them. When I remember a story they shared months ago, they know I was listening. Memory is a language of relationships, not simply a storage device.

For years, I assumed these lapses were simply a part of growing older. Then I realised it wasn’t just me.

I see young people interrupting conversations to search for facts they probably know. Colleagues looking up phone numbers they have dialled for years. Children depending on GPS to find places they visit regularly. They forget names and details as much as I do. Perhaps this isn’t about age at all.

A little browsing revealed that researchers call this the Google effect or digital amnesia. When we know information can be retrieved instantly from a device, our brains make less effort to remember it. Gradually, we become better at remembering where information is stored than the information itself.

I am not suggesting that technology is the villain. Far from it. My phone has made life easier in countless ways. But somewhere along the way, it has quietly become an extension of my memory.

That made me ask myself a simple question. Are there some memories I should never outsource? For me, the answer is yes.

The phone numbers of the people I love. The names of people who matter. The birthdays of dear ones. The route to a friend’s house. A few poems, songs and prayers that have become a part of me. The stories that bind me to family and friends. Not because my phone cannot remember them. But because I need to remember them to reach out and relate to the people who matter to me, without the mediation of a device.

title: The shrill roads of Delhi
author: Sunanda Bharti
content_html:
Perhaps it is time to remove the words “Horn Please” or “Blow Horn” from the back of trucks and other vehicles. What may once have been a practical instruction now appears to function as a psychological trigger.

The typical Delhi driver approaches the horn with the enthusiasm of a pianist discovering a new keyboard.

So, the average Delhi motorist does not need encouragement to honk, but something opposite.

There are, broadly speaking, three kinds of drivers on Delhi’s roads. The first drives a vehicle with no brakes, putting any bullet train to shame. The second drives a vehicle with no accelerator, making a buffalo cart look positively dynamic.

The third, and by far the most fascinating species, drives a vehicle powered almost entirely by the horn.

Petrol, diesel and CNG are useful, certainly, but secondary. The horn is the principal fuel source. The remarkable thing is that honking in Delhi has long ceased to be a warning device. It has become a language, a coping mechanism, and perhaps even a form of therapy. One honk says, “Move.” Two honks say, “Move faster.” A sustained blast says, “I am deeply dissatisfied with the state of the nation!” The horn has become the preferred medium through which citizens express their views on traffic congestion, potholes, road construction, governance, weather conditions, and occasionally the meaninglessness of existence while caught in traffic jams. Tourists are often bewildered upon being greeted by what appears to be a city-wide percussion orchestra. Their confusion deepens when they encounter signs outside schools and hospitals declaring “No Honking”. To the average Delhi driver, this sign seems to be interpreted not as a prohibition but as a polite suggestion, much like a New Year’s resolution.

This has led me to a policy proposal. Motor manufacturers should begin installing horns with an expiry limit. Every vehicle may be entitled to a thousand complimentary honks. Thereafter, the horn ceases to function until it is recharged.

The first recharge may be reasonably priced.

Every subsequent recharge should attract a premium. A portion of the proceeds could be dedicated to combating noise pollution in the capital.

After all, governments frequently use taxation and regulation to shape public behaviour. We tax tobacco. We discourage plastic. We regulate emissions. Why not regulate recreational honking? And if a small surcharge persuades even a fraction of Delhi’s motorists to discover the existence of patience, and silence, the city might finally hear something it has not heard in years. Peace and quiet.

title: The price of greatness: what the world did not see in Rafael Nadal
author: N. Anand Venkatesh
content_html:
The German writer Goethe once wrote a truth that cuts straight to the bone: “Talent is built in calm; character is built in the storm.” Look around today, and you will see a world entirely obsessed with the calm. We are taught to seek comfort, to avoid friction, and to build protective, fragile bubbles around our lives to keep any hint of discomfort away. We treat pain as a stop sign — a signal to quit, pack up, and run. But the Netflix’s documentary series RAFA completely shatters this illusion.

It doesn’t just show us a glamorous montage of trophies and roaring crowds, but it introduces us to a man who chose to live, fight, and win from the very centre of a brutal, lifelong storm. For the youth of today, who are so often shielded from hardship, this story is not about tennis. It is a masterclass in how to take the worst life throws at you and use it as fuel to become unstoppable.

To truly understand Rafael Nadal, you have to look at the hidden cracks beneath his greatness. Early in his career, a devastating medical reality threatened to destroy his dream before it even started. He was diagnosed with Müller-Weiss syndrome — a rare, painful, and permanent condition that causes the bone in his foot to literally waste away. The top medical experts gave him a cold, simple choice: undergo surgery, and accept that your career as a professional athlete is over.

At that crossroads, most people would have taken the comfortable exit. Rafa chose the storm. He refused the surgery and his team came up with a temporary, desperate fix which is an extra layer of custom foam stuffed inside his shoe. It was a fragile Band-Aid on a broken body. The extra foam changed how he ran, sending a chain reaction of intense stress up into his knees, his hamstrings, and his back. From that moment on, Nadal was at war with his own body.

His coaches and his family lived in constant anxiety. Year after year, the news behind closed doors was almost always bad. Another tear, another flare-up, another joint giving out. Yet, time and time again, Rafa would look past the medical data, ignore the screaming protests of his nerves, step onto the court, and beat the best players in the world.

This madness reached its peak during his historic run at the French Open. To compete on the brutal clay courts, Nadal did something that defies human logic. He chose to completely numb his foot using constant, aggressive nerve-block injections. Think about the sheer mental toughness required to step onto a global stage, facing the fiercest competitors on earth, while being entirely unable to feel the foot connecting you to the ground. He was running on pure muscle memory, instinct, and an iron will. He was surviving on painkillers, yet he marched through the tournament to lift the championship trophy.

The world often looked at Nadal’s rigid on-court habits in the way he perfectly aligned his water bottles, swept the baseline, or fixed his clothes before every single serve and laughed, calling it superstition. But the truth is much deeper. When your physical body is burning in agony, strict routine is how you take control back from the chaos. Those habits were his mental shield, a way to drown out the white noise of pain so his mind could focus entirely on the next ball.

There is a dangerous lie being fed to the next generation: that a successful life is supposed to be an easy, painless one. We celebrate the finish line but completely erase the bloody footprints it took to get there. Young people see a champion holding a golden trophy under a shower of confetti, completely blind to the hundreds of hours that same champion spent crying on a treatment table, surrounded by a worried family and an anxious team.

We must show youngsters this story to teach them that pain is not a dead end. It can be a massive spark. Nadal proved that suffering does not have to break you and that it can reveal exactly what you are made of. He showed the world that when you stop running from discomfort, you take away its power over you. Eventually, as it does to everyone, time delivered its final verdict. The body could simply take no more, the foam insoles and nerve blocks could no longer bridge the gap, and he had to retire. But Rafael Nadal did not leave the sport because he was broken but he left because he had completely emptied the tank. He left every single ounce of his humanity on the court.

If we want to build a generation capable of surviving hard times and achieving true greatness, we have to teach them to stop hiding in the calm. True character is only built when you have the courage to look directly into the eyes of the storm, smile through the pain, and refuse to back down.

N. Anand Venkatesh is a judge of the Madras High Court
